keyVerseText: And Elijah the Tishbite, who was of the inhabitants of Gilead, said unto Ahab, As the LORD God of Israel liveth, before whom I stand, there shall not be dew nor rain these years, but according to my word. Elijah: Heb. Elijahu: Gr. Elias
rootMeaning: The word תִּשְׁבִּי (Tishbîy) is a patrial noun derived from an unused place name meaning 'recourse.' This suggests that the original sense of the term relates to a person belonging to a location that may have been understood as a place of refuge or source of help. The literal or root sense thus adds a dimension of identity tied to a specific geographic and perhaps spiritual heritage, beyond the simple English gloss 'the Tishbite.'
usageInScripture: The term תִּשְׁבִּי appears six times in Scripture, consistently translated as 'the Tishbite.' It identifies Elijah as an inhabitant of Tishbeh in Gilead, although the exact site and name remain uncertain. This consistent usage as a gentilic adjective highlights the importance of Elijah's regional origin, grounding his prophetic identity in a particular community and cultural context.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding תִּשְׁבִּי as a designation tied to a specific locale enriches our appreciation of Elijah not merely as an isolated prophet but as one deeply rooted in the history and geography of God's covenant people. His identity as 'the Tishbite' underscores God's use of ordinary, local individuals to fulfill divine purposes, emphasizing that God’s work often arises from particular places and peoples. This reflects the evangelical truth that God calls and empowers believers within their unique contexts to serve His kingdom faithfully. Moreover, the notion of 'recourse' embedded in the name points to God as the ultimate refuge and source of help, a theme central to Christian faith.
keyVerseReflection: In 1 Kings 17:1, Elijah is introduced as 'Elijah the Tishbite, who was of the inhabitants of Gilead,' emphasizing his rootedness in a specific place. This designation grounds Elijah’s prophetic authority in his identity and heritage. When he declares the drought 'before whom I stand,' the word תִּשְׁבִּי reminds readers that this prophet is not a nameless figure but a real person from a real community, called by God to speak His word with authority and power.
